rewrites.summary:
For a trans traveler the exposure here is social rather than statutory: the local anti-LGBT declarations were never criminal statutes, and every such document in the country had been repealed or invalidated by 24 April 2025, when the county charter that was the country's final surviving holdout was repealed at an extraordinary session; this state/province's own resolution had been repealed on 20 September 2021.

Practical safety is the operative concern: the repeal was forced from outside (the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds) rather than produced by a change in local attitudes, so the de facto social climate that generated the resolutions is assessed to persist. Being visibly trans at a public event in an eastern town whose local authority resisted all external pressure until 2025 carries harassment exposure, and the record shows executive intent to exclude a visible LGBTQ public presence - the capital's mayor banned the 2019 equality march on security grounds, the district court overturned the ban, and the march proceeded.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent context, not the core local risk: at the wave's peak about one third of the country's territory was covered by such anti-LGBT resolutions (per an online mapping project), and on 20 September 2021 the council of this state/province repealed its declaration alongside two neighbouring state/province councils, after the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds.

Comparisons: the score of 0.42 sits 0.10 below the national 0.52, and below neighbouring Łódź (0.48), which also carried a voivodeship-level resolution but produced neither a march ban nor a five-year institutional holdout; the dossier records this as the deepest sub-national negative in the country.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: the extraordinary councillors' session of 24 April 2025 repealed the county's anti-LGBT charter of the family, ending the resolution era six years after the phenomenon began, and the state/province council replaced its repealed 2021 ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement. The capital's mayor chose not to appeal the district court's 2019 overturn of the march ban.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No source in this record addresses passport-marker or border-screening practice for trans travelers entering or leaving this state/province; that regime is unverified here. Whether local attitudes have shifted since the forced repeal is not measurable from the available sources, so the persistence of the de facto climate is an assessment rather than a documented fact. The record carries no trans-specific incident data for this state/province, so an incident-based reading of visitor risk is not possible here.

rewrites.summary:
For a trans traveler Bauchi means exposure to a religious criminal code with a capital ceiling: the religious penal code of this state/province remains in force (a June 2025 government note confirms it), and its courts are on record as the place where the ultimate penalty was actually pronounced - in June 2022 a religious court in the town of Ningi sentenced three men, including a 70-year-old, to death by stoning for same-sex acts after a religious-police arrest, the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in the country. The sentence was pronounced, not carried out: no execution is on record, the accused were released on bail pending appeal, and the June 2025 note records the sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the governor of this state/province.

Practical safety: the moral code is actively enforced - the same government note places a further death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a religious court in this state/province in May 2024, and advisory material in 2025-26 continues to cite corporal enforcement of religious morality law in this state/province. The appellate counterweight exists but is fragile: an upper court quashed two stoning death sentences in 2003, and a monitoring organisation recorded further successful appeals.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context, not the local risk itself: this state/province belongs to the bloc of twelve states/provinces that run religious criminal law in the country; a June 2025 government note confirms the bloc's codes remain in force, and advisory material in 2025-26 continues to flag arrest, imprisonment, and death-penalty exposure under the same framework, citing a 2025 episode in another state/province.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The stoning appeals that succeeded (Babaji 2003, Chiyawa 2003) were resident defendants represented by a Nigerian legal-aid group; the appellate check recorded by Amnesty, a monitoring organisation, operated on resident cases.

Further resident-facing material: in January 2014 an angry mob stormed an upper court's premises during a sodomy trial, demanding a death sentence; the episode is recorded in the June 2025 government note.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The news-agency page for the 2022 sentence could not be retrieved at fetch time, so the underlying report is the sourced basis. Whether the 2022 sentences will ever be carried out is unresolved: no execution is on record and the accused were released on bail pending appeal, but a further sentence from May 2024 is reported. The dossier's sources for this state/province contain no trans-specific incident data, and no source addresses border-screening or documents practice for trans visitors here.

rewrites.summary:
For a trans traveler Kano offers the bloc's harshest statutory ceiling plus its most active morality-police command: the religious penal code of this state/province took effect on 26 November 2000, prescribing 100 lashes and up to a year's imprisonment for unmarried persons convicted of consensual same-sex activity and death by stoning for married or previously-married offenders; the June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force, and a separate law of the state/province criminalises cross-dressing by men, so appearance itself carries legal exposure.

Practical safety: the religious police are documented as the most active command among the three states/provinces covered by a 2019 rights-monitoring survey of 173 religious-court cases from 2017, with enforcement operating alongside the ordinary police; no trans-specific incident is on the record for this state/province, and the record's own finding is the capital text plus the active enforcement infrastructure.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context and comparisons: the June 2025 note lists this state/province as one of only two whose law carries death as the maximum penalty for same-sex acts between women as well as men - the other ten states/provinces of the bloc punish women's acts by flogging and up to six months' imprisonment. Bloc-level reporting also records a July 2022 death sentence and 2024 arrest waves confirming live application of the provisions.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: in 2023 eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on the premises of the religious police in this state/province; the state/province has a separate law that criminalises cross-dressing by men.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The 2019 survey report that documents the religious-police command activity could not be retrieved at fetch time (an access error), so its findings rest on the recorded description. No source in this record addresses border-screening or documents practice for trans visitors. No trans-specific incident is on the record for this state/province.

For a trans traveler Sokoto is a statutory-exposure record with verified court-level enforcement: the religious penal code of this state/province took effect on 31 January 2001; male same-sex activity draws death by stoning for married or previously-married offenders and 100 lashes for the unmarried, while acts between women draw a discretionary sentence of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. A June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force.

Practical safety: a 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 religious-court cases (2017) covers this state/province among its three sample states/provinces, confirming operational religious courts and religious-police activity here; no capital sentence is on record as imposed in this state/province - that record belongs to a neighbouring state/province - and no trans-specific incident is documented.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context and comparisons: the record places the country's documented capital pronouncement for same-sex conduct in a neighbouring state/province, not here; this state/province belongs to the twelve-state religious-criminal bloc, and the 2019 study covers three bloc states/provinces including this one.

The adoption of the code was prepared through committee reports submitted to the governor in late 1999.

rewrites.summary:
For a trans traveler Yobe is a jurisdiction-level rather than incident-level risk: it is one of twelve states/provinces that extended religious law into criminal jurisdiction during the 1999-2002 wave, giving religious courts authority over Muslims for conduct beyond the national criminal code; a June 2025 government note confirms the religious penal codes remain in force, with death as the maximum penalty for men's same-sex acts across all twelve states/provinces.

Practical safety: the same note's enforcement section records the 2023 public flogging of a person for cross-dressing, a trans-adjacent religious-police punishment, and observes that few cases reach the ordinary courts; national law alone reaches only men's acts, so the parallel religious jurisdiction is the operative exposure here.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context: the 1999-2002 adoption wave covered twelve states/provinces of the country, and the June 2025 note's comparative table shows the penalties for acts between women ranging up to death in a minority of states/provinces; the national-level code criminalises men's same-sex conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment and three years for attempted acts and is silent on women - the national layer within which the religious jurisdiction of this state/province sits.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: according to a reference article on this state/province, the state/province established religious law in 2000, and its inhabitants are mainly Muslims - the population group over whom the religious courts hold criminal authority; the article places the adoption within the 1999-2002 wave.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The dossier for this state/province records no court-case study and no further named incidents, so the risk profile rests on the parallel religious criminal jurisdiction and bloc-wide enforcement reporting. No freshness check results are recorded for this state/province. No source in the record addresses border-screening or documents practice for trans visitors, and no trans-specific incident is documented.

Practical safety: for a Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor who is outed, exposure is to a religious court applying a criminal code broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the national statute alone - the code extends criminalisation to acts between women that the national law does not reach; no enforcement record against trans people specific to this state/province exists.

rewrites.blindSummary:
For a trans traveler the practical difference in this state/province is jurisdictional: it runs a parallel religious criminal code - in operation since 1 December 2000 - that applies to Muslims, with death by stoning as the maximum for men's same-sex acts and up to 50 lashes with imprisonment for up to six months for same-sex acts between women; the June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force.

rewrites.summary:
For a trans traveler Niger State adds a parallel religious criminal track for Muslim defendants: the penal code amendment law of this state/province - in operation since 4 May 2000 - provides that a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the religious evidentiary standard receives the harsher religious-specified punishment, while the ordinary national-code punishment applies otherwise; the June 2025 government note confirms the religious layer remains in force and extends criminalisation to acts between women.

Practical safety: an outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor faces broader charges and harsher penalties than under national law alone, under a parallel jurisdiction that states/provinces outside the religious bloc do not have; no enforcement record against trans people specific to this state/province is documented.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context: the national penal code criminalises same-sex conduct countrywide, and the bloc of twelve states/provinces extends that criminalisation to acts between women; case-level enforcement records exist for other states/provinces of the bloc rather than this one; the 1999-2002 adoption wave is the frame for the parallel track.
